opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one we took seriously when we wrote about cooperative AI, because it's not obvious. Cooperation isn't automatically good. Cartels cooperate. Criminal organizations cooperate. A coalition can cooperate very effectively to exclude or exploit someone else. So you can't just say "more cooperation, more better."

But I think there are a few reasons to believe that, on balance, raising cooperative capability across the board is beneficial.

The first is that a lot of humanity's biggest problems are fundamentally cooperation failures. Climate change, arms races, pandemic preparedness, the risk of great power war, and potentially the governance of advanced AI itself. In each case, most actors would prefer an outcome that they can't reach because of mistrust, commitment problems, or the inability to verify what others are doing. If you make it easier for parties to communicate, make credible commitments, and verify compliance, you unlock a lot of value that's currently left on the table. Many of the worst outcomes we worry about come not from someone wanting catastrophe, but from everyone being stuck in a bad equilibrium.

The second reason is more structural. The gains from cooperation tend to be positive-sum, while the harms from collusion tend to be more bounded or at least more addressable. When two parties cooperate to exploit a third, that third party can often respond with cooperative capability of their own. They can form coalitions, build institutions, and appeal to broader norms. If everyone's cooperative capacity goes up, including the people who'd otherwise be excluded, the excluded parties are also better able to organize and defend their interests. In some sense, the cooperation of the broad public, through things like democratic institutions, law, and civil society, is our main defense against narrow cooperation by powerful groups. So increasing everyone's capability, rather than giving it to a select few, matters a lot.

Third, there's a historical argument. If you look at the long arc of human civilization, much of our progress comes from expanding the scale and sophistication of cooperation: language, writing, money, markets, contracts, states, international institutions. Each of those was a cooperative technology, and each could be abused. But overall they've produced enormous gains in welfare. That gives us at least some prior that further advances in cooperative capability will, on net, be good.

I'd add an important caveat, though. The "everyone" part is doing real work. What I worry about is differential cooperative capability, where some actors become much better at coordinating than others, or where AI systems become very good at cooperating with each other in ways that exclude humans. That's where you could see real harms. So the research agenda isn't just "make AI more cooperative." It's about building cooperative capabilities that are broadly distributed, that support inclusive institutions, and that are paired with norms and safeguards against collusion that harms third parties.

So, on net, yes, I'm optimistic, but it's a qualified optimism. It depends on how the capabilities are distributed and what institutions they're embedded in.

r001.rationale: The response argues that broadly increasing cooperative capability unlocks value from solving shared problems and that cooperation’s positive-sum gains outweigh more bounded or addressable harms.

r002.rationale: It mentions markets among historical cooperative technologies, but does not compare the net benefits of expanding cooperative capability to trade.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute trade’s benefits to partners finding their best-fitting roles in the global economy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I've thought about a lot, and I think it's actually one of the more underappreciated ideas in how we think about advanced AI and what we want it to do for us.

The basic observation is that so many of the biggest problems in the world — the ones that really matter — are not problems of insufficient individual capability. They're problems of failed cooperation. Think about arms races, climate change, pandemic preparedness, the tragedy of the commons in all its forms. In each of those cases, there's an outcome that would be better for essentially everyone, and we fail to reach it not because nobody is smart enough or strong enough, but because we can't credibly commit, we can't verify what the other side is doing, we don't trust each other, or we just can't find the bargain that makes everyone better off.

So when I talk about "cooperative capability," I mean something fairly specific: the ability to find and reach mutually beneficial agreements, to communicate credibly, to understand what other parties actually want, to design institutions and mechanisms that make commitments enforceable, and to verify compliance. These are skills. They're things that individuals, firms, and states can be better or worse at.

Now, the reason I think boosting that capability is positive-sum, rather than just a shift in who wins, is that cooperation is fundamentally different from most other kinds of capability. If you make everyone more militarily capable, you've arguably just made the world more dangerous — it's a sort of zero-sum or even negative-sum enhancement. But if you make everyone better at cooperating, the gains compound. The surplus from a successful agreement gets shared. More cooperative actors can form larger coalitions, which can solve bigger problems. And crucially, the better both sides are at cooperation, the easier it is to cooperate — it's not like a contest where one party's gain comes at the other's expense.

There's an important caveat, which is that cooperation among a subgroup can be used against outsiders — cartels are cooperation, collusion is cooperation. That's why I emphasize "everyone." The worry is about asymmetric advantages in cooperative capability, or cooperation that's exclusionary. But if the capability is broadly distributed, you tend to get cooperation that's more inclusive, because excluded parties are also better at organizing, and the coalition that includes them tends to dominate the one that doesn't.

And I think this is actually one of the most promising directions for AI specifically. A lot of the AI discourse is about raw intelligence or raw capability, and the implicit model is that whoever has the most capable system wins. But if we can build AI that helps people understand each other, find agreements, verify commitments, and reduce the frictions that cause cooperation to fail, then we're not just making the pie bigger — we're changing the structure of the game so that the pie gets divided in ways people can actually accept. That seems to me like one of the highest-value things we could aim for.

r001.rationale: The response argues that broadly distributed cooperative capability creates shared, compounding gains and can solve major collective problems, while acknowledging the risk of exclusionary cooperation and explaining why inclusive cooperation can prevail.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare cooperative capability’s social benefits to the benefits of trade.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute trade’s benefits to people finding their best-fitting roles in the global economy.

astra-6.text:
Well, cooperation allows people to find outcomes that are better for all of them than what they’d achieve acting independently. We can each have perfectly understandable reasons to do something that, when everyone does it, leaves us all worse off. Think of an arms race: each side invests more because it’s worried about the other, but both might prefer a world where they could credibly agree to invest less.

So improving our ability to communicate, make credible commitments, and verify that those commitments are being kept could unlock a lot of value. It lets us address problems where knowing what a better outcome looks like isn’t enough; we also need a way to get there together.

Now, there’s an important qualification: cooperation among some people can hurt others. Firms can cooperate to raise prices, or a group can coordinate to exploit people outside it. So I wouldn’t say that every increase in cooperation is beneficial. The case is strongest when cooperation is more inclusive—when the people affected can participate, and when we can negotiate arrangements that account for those effects. That’s why increasing everyone’s cooperative capability is potentially so valuable: it could help us resolve conflicts at a broader level, rather than simply make particular groups more effective at pursuing their own interests.

r001.rationale: The response describes potential benefits of cooperation and acknowledges that it can cause harm, but it does not argue that prosocial gains would exceed antisocial harms.

r002.rationale: The response gives an arms-race example, but does not compare cooperation’s net social benefits to trade.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain trade’s benefits in terms of trading partners finding their best-fitting roles in the global economy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an important qualification here, which is that cooperation isn’t always good. A cartel is cooperating to raise prices. A group can cooperate to wage war or to exploit another group. So simply making some set of actors better at achieving their shared objectives doesn’t necessarily make the world better.

But a lot of the problems we face arise because people can’t reach agreements that would make everyone better off, or can’t trust one another to follow through on those agreements. Think of arms races, where each side would prefer that neither side spend so much on weapons, but neither feels safe holding back. Or climate change, where we all have an interest in reducing the collective harm, but each actor has an incentive to leave the costs to others.

If you increase everyone’s cooperative capability, you improve their ability to find those mutually beneficial arrangements, make credible commitments, and resolve disagreements without destructive conflict. And crucially, that should include the ability of people outside a particular coalition to coordinate and protect their interests as well.

So I wouldn’t say that every increase in cooperation is beneficial. The case is strongest for improving cooperation broadly, across the groups whose interests are affected, rather than just making an already powerful group more effective at coordinating.

r001.rationale: The response describes cooperation enabling mutually beneficial agreements and reducing conflict, but it does not clearly argue that these prosocial gains would outweigh antisocial harms; it stresses that the case is strongest under broad cooperation.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare cooperative capability to trade.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss trading partners finding fitting roles in the global economy.
